===========================================================================
CardDemo - Grafana overview dashboard
===========================================================================

PROVENANCE
  Legacy estate checkout SHA : 7756d895ffeb65f7ea72aaa609e356d9899afcec
  Upstream release stamp     : CardDemo_v1.0-15-g27d6c6f-68 (2022-07-19)

  That stamp is the DESIGNATED provenance identifier for this migration and
  the one carried by the dominant cohort of legacy members. It is not the
  only stamp in the estate - three further stamps appear on a small number
  of members - so it is cited as the designated identifier rather than as a
  universal one.

  This file has no legacy antecedent. Nothing in the mainframe estate
  corresponds to it, so it is a net-new artifact rather than the translation
  of a COBOL program, a copybook or a job stream. Traceability is by
  CITATION only - path and line number - and no legacy source text is
  reproduced anywhere in this module.

PURPOSE
  This is the presentation surface of the observability layer that replaces
  the legacy estate's only diagnostic channel, the DISPLAY statement -
  approximately 217 of them across the 28 COBOL programs. The count is
  deliberately approximate: it varies with parse tolerance, and a raw keyword
  grep over the legacy tree reports a higher figure than a statement-context
  parse does, so no exact number is asserted here.

  Collection is config/prometheus/prometheus.yml, which scrapes
  /actuator/prometheus and stamps job="carddemo-app" onto every series it
  collects. Resolution is
  config/grafana/provisioning/datasources/datasource.yml, which publishes
  uid "carddemo-prometheus". Every panel below names that uid and every
  query below filters on that job label. Both strings are interfaces between
  files rather than local choices: change either one on a single side and
  every panel here empties while the whole stack still reports healthy.

  The job label is used in preference to the application meter tag because
  it describes scrape topology. That collector also scrapes itself under a
  second job, so an unfiltered query would mix two targets.

PERFORMANCE GATE - THIS DASHBOARD ESTABLISHES A BASELINE AND ASSERTS NONE
  Gate 3 ESTABLISHES the first Java performance baseline. These panels
  present measurements only. No panel asserts a service level, and no
  numeric latency, throughput, availability or capacity figure exists
  anywhere in the source estate - not in the COBOL, not in the job streams,
  not in the CICS resource definitions - so there is nothing for a panel to
  be checked against. Recorded figures are written up in
  docs/gate-evidence.md.

  The three figures the gate names are all read from here: elapsed time from
  the batch job and step timers, peak memory from the peak-heap panel, and
  records per second from the item-read rate.

  That is why no panel carries a threshold ladder, a limit line, an alert
  rule or a fixed axis range. Percentiles, rates and windowed peaks are
  INSTRUMENTATION and are exactly what is wanted; a boundary drawn across
  any of them would fabricate a service level this migration is expressly
  forbidden from inventing. Their absence is a decision, not an oversight,
  and a reader who finds the panels bare should read that as intent.

DISPLAY CADENCE IS NOT A SERVICE LEVEL
  "refresh" is how often a browser re-runs these queries and "time" is the
  window the panels cover. Both are viewing preferences that belong to
  whoever is looking. Neither states anything about how fast the application
  is or ought to be, and neither should be read as a limit by a reviewer
  applying the no-capacity-figure rule.

BATCH SERIES ARE ABSENT UNTIL A JOB IS LAUNCHED
  spring.batch.job.enabled is false in application.yml, so no job runs at
  application startup. Spring Batch series come into existence only after a
  job has been launched through the module's batch job launch endpoint,
  com.carddemo.api.BatchJobController. An empty batch row before the first
  launch is EXPECTED, not a defect.

  The same holds for the application-registered meters row: a Micrometer
  meter is created on first use, so each of those series appears only once
  its emitting path has actually executed.

FIXTURE VOLUMES THE BASELINE IS MEASURED OVER
  Daily transactions : 300 records, 105,300 bytes - 250 point-of-sale
                       purchases and 50 operator-originated returns. All 300
                       carry the same processing date and the same
                       timestamp, so date-window filtering has to be
                       exercised by a separately constructed fixture rather
                       than by this input.
  Accounts           : 50 records
  Category balances  : 50 records - the interest run's driving set
  Disclosure groups  : 51 records

  A figure read off these panels is only meaningful when it is quoted
  alongside these volumes, which is why they are recorded here rather than
  left to the reader to rediscover.

SCOPE - THE LOCAL VALIDATION STACK AND NOTHING ELSE
  Grafana reads this file from /var/lib/grafana/dashboards, where the
  sibling docker-compose.yml mounts config/grafana/dashboards read-only, and
  the provider definition in config/grafana/provisioning/dashboards places
  it in the CardDemo folder with UI updates disabled - so this file, not the
  browser, is the source of truth.

  This file presents NO credential of any kind. Grafana's own sign-in values
  come from the compose environment, and a 401 answered by the scrape
  endpoint would be a matter for com.carddemo.config.SecurityConfig, never
  something to resolve by committing a credential to this repository.
===========================================================================

panels.description: One endpoint group per legacy screen transaction. Five admin-gated transactions and one public sign-on transaction are among them. Every series here is published by Spring Boot Actuator, so these panels have data as soon as one request has been served.
panels.title: Per-endpoint - REST surface of the CICS screen transactions

panels.description: Requests per second, split by URI and method. Framework-published counter, so it needs no application instrumentation.
panels.title: Request rate by endpoint

panels.description: Requests per second whose outcome was not SUCCESS, split by status so a client fault reads differently from a server fault.

targets.expr: sum by (uri, method, status) (rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{job="$job", uri=~"$uri", outcome!="SUCCESS"}[$__rate_interval]))

panels.title: Error rate by endpoint

panels.description: Non-SUCCESS rate divided by total rate. A proportion that is observed, not one that is required.

targets.expr: sum by (uri) (rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{job="$job", uri=~"$uri", outcome!="SUCCESS"}[$__rate_interval])) / sum by (uri) (rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{job="$job", uri=~"$uri"}[$__rate_interval]))

panels.title: Error ratio by endpoint

panels.description: Read off the percentile histogram that application.yml enables for the request timer. These are MEASUREMENTS of what happened, not levels anything is held to, which is why the panel carries no limit line.
panels.title: Observed request latency percentiles - p50, p95, p99

panels.description: Timer sum rate over timer count rate. The arithmetic mean over the refresh window, reported alongside the percentiles because the two answer different questions.

targets.expr: sum by (uri) (rate(http_server_requests_seconds_sum{job="$job", uri=~"$uri"}[$__rate_interval])) / sum by (uri) (rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{job="$job", uri=~"$uri"}[$__rate_interval]))

panels.title: Observed mean request latency by endpoint

panels.description: The framework's own decaying maximum for the request timer. Useful for spotting a single slow call the percentiles smooth away.
panels.title: Observed recent maximum request latency by endpoint

panels.description: Nine job configurations carry the application work of the legacy job streams; the remaining steps in those streams were dataset definition and utility invocations, which became schema migrations, in-job comparators and compose services rather than batch steps. There is no master orchestrator: ordering across the pipeline is an operational convention. One job is defined without a legacy driver and is excluded from the default pipeline, so it appears here only when a test launches it. EVERY series in this row is absent until a job has been launched.
panels.title: Per-batch-step - Spring Batch jobs replacing the application job steps

panels.description: Maximum and mean wall-clock duration per job. This is where the Gate 3 elapsed-time figure is read. Quote it with the fixture volumes recorded in this dashboard's description. Absent until a job has been launched.
panels.title: Batch job elapsed time - GATE 3 ELAPSED TIME

panels.description: Maximum and mean duration per step, keyed by owning job and step name. Absent until a job has been launched.

targets.expr: sum by (spring_batch_step_job_name, spring_batch_step_name) (spring_batch_step_seconds_sum{job="$job", spring_batch_step_name=~"$step"}) / sum by (spring_batch_step_job_name, spring_batch_step_name) (spring_batch_step_seconds_count{job="$job", spring_batch_step_name=~"$step"})

panels.title: Batch step elapsed time

panels.description: Rate of the item-read timer's count, which is one observation per record read. This is where the Gate 3 records-per-second figure is read. Note that this timer's labels are unprefixed, unlike the job and step timers above. Absent until a job has been launched.
panels.title: Records read per second - GATE 3 RECORDS PER SECOND

panels.description: Increase in the item-read count across whatever window the time picker is showing. A volume observed, never a volume expected.
panels.title: Records read over the selected window

panels.description: Cumulative job-timer count split by status. Spring Batch 5.2.6 publishes no active-job gauge, so execution counts by status are the available view of job outcomes over time.
panels.title: Batch job executions by status

panels.description: One row per job, step and status. The status label distinguishes a step that completed from one that failed, which is the distinction the legacy condition-code gating depended on.
panels.title: Batch step executions by status

panels.description: Published by Micrometer's JVM and process binders, so this row has data from application startup onward and needs no request or job to populate it. Axes are left auto-scaled on purpose: a fixed range would imply an acceptable band, and none is documented anywhere in the source estate.
panels.title: JVM and process - GATE 3 PEAK MEMORY is read from this row

panels.description: Used against committed against the maximum the JVM reports. The maximum is a fact the runtime publishes about itself, not a limit asserted here; no heap sizing figure is set by this module.

targets.legendFormat: heap max reported by the JVM

panels.title: Heap used, committed and maximum

panels.description: The largest summed heap occupancy seen anywhere in the window the time picker is showing. This is where the Gate 3 peak-memory figure is read. It is a measurement over a chosen window, so widen the window before quoting it and record it beside the fixture volumes.
panels.title: Peak heap over the selected window - GATE 3 PEAK MEMORY

panels.description: Metaspace, compressed class space and the code heaps. Reported per pool as well as in total, because a class-space trend and a code-cache trend mean different things.
panels.title: Non-heap used by pool

panels.description: Pauses per second and pause-seconds per second, split by action and cause. The second series is a dimensionless proportion of wall-clock time spent paused.
panels.title: Garbage-collection pause rate and pause time

panels.description: Process and whole-system processor usage on the left axis, live thread count on the right. No thread-count figure is configured by this module, so the count is observed rather than bounded.
panels.title: Processor usage and live threads

panels.description: Seconds since this process started. Reported so that a figure read from the other panels can be placed against how long the process had been running when it was taken. It is not an availability proportion and no availability proportion is asserted anywhere in this dashboard.
panels.title: Process uptime observed

panels.description: Observation only. The HikariCP 6.3.3 default configuration is retained DELIBERATELY because no legacy tuning baseline exists to tune against: every legacy data file was defined with uncommitted read integrity and no recovery, so there is no prior figure for pool behaviour. These panels exist to be read, and no pool size, timeout or concurrency figure is set by this module.
panels.title: Connection pool - OBSERVATION ONLY, not a tuning surface

panels.description: Active, idle and pending connections per pool. Pending rising while active is flat is the shape worth noticing; no figure is prescribed for any of the three.
panels.title: Connection pool activity

panels.description: Restates, for anyone reading the dashboard rather than its JSON, what the performance gate does and does not do.
panels.title: How to read this dashboard

panels.description: The same framing carried in this dashboard's own description, repeated on the canvas so it is read by someone who never opens the file.

options.content:
## Gate 3 establishes the first Java performance baseline. It asserts no threshold.

No numeric latency, throughput, availability or capacity figure exists anywhere in the
legacy estate - not in the COBOL, not in the job streams, not in the CICS resource
definitions - so there is nothing here for a panel to be checked against. **These panels
measure.** Recorded figures are written up in `docs/gate-evidence.md`.

### Where each of the three figures the gate names is read

| Gate 3 figure | Panel |
| --- | --- |
| Elapsed time | *Batch job elapsed time*, and *Batch step elapsed time* |
| Peak memory | *Peak heap over the selected window* |
| Records per second | *Records read per second* |

### Quote every figure alongside the fixture volumes it was measured over

- **Daily transactions - 300 records, 105,300 bytes.** 250 point-of-sale purchases and
  50 operator-originated returns, so both signed directions of the balance computation
  are exercised. All 300 carry the same processing date and the same timestamp, so
  date-window filtering has to be exercised by a separately constructed fixture rather
  than by this input.
- **Accounts - 50 records.**
- **Transaction-category balances - 50 records.** The interest run's driving set.
- **Disclosure groups - 51 records.** Three complete groups, one of which is the default
  group, which is what makes both the direct-hit and the fallback branch of the interest
  lookup reachable from seeded data alone.

A number taken from these panels without those volumes beside it is not a baseline.

### Batch rows are empty until a job is launched

`spring.batch.job.enabled` is `false`, so no job runs at application startup. Spring
Batch series come into existence only once a job has been launched through the module's
batch job launch endpoint. The application-registered meters row behaves the same way,
because a Micrometer meter is created on first use. **An empty panel before the first
run is expected, not a defect.**

### Why there is no threshold, no limit line and no alert rule here

Percentiles, rates and windowed peaks are instrumentation. A boundary drawn across one
of them would be a service level, and this migration is expressly forbidden from
inventing one. `refresh` and `time` are display cadence and display window - viewing
preferences, not limits.

### Provenance

Legacy estate checkout SHA `7756d895ffeb65f7ea72aaa609e356d9899afcec`; upstream release
stamp `CardDemo_v1.0-15-g27d6c6f-68` (2022-07-19), the designated provenance identifier
for this migration. Traceability is by citation - path and line number - and no legacy
source text is reproduced anywhere in this module.

panels.title: Gate 3 - baseline, fixture volumes, and why there are no thresholds

panels.description: Unlike the rows above, these four meters are registered by this module's own code rather than by the framework, and Micrometer creates a meter on first use. Each panel here is therefore EXPECTED to be empty until the path that emits it has actually executed. Every name below was verified against a real registration in the module source; no metric this module does not emit is charted anywhere in this dashboard.
panels.title: Application-registered meters - SECONDARY, each present only once its code path has run

panels.description: One observation per run of a translated batch program, tagged with the legacy program name and whether the lifecycle completed or abended. The abended outcome is the translation of the legacy terminal path, so a series appearing under it is a real failure rather than a slow run.

targets.expr: sum by (step, outcome) (carddemo_batch_cobol_step_seconds_sum{job="$job"}) / sum by (step, outcome) (carddemo_batch_cobol_step_seconds_count{job="$job"})

panels.title: Legacy batch program lifecycle elapsed time

panels.description: Records written to the fixed-length reject dataset, as a rate on the left axis and as a window total on the right. Rejects are an expected product of the posting validation cascade, not an error condition, so no acceptable count is stated for them.
panels.title: Reject-record write throughput

panels.description: Duration of one chunk write to the reject dataset, tagged by resource and by whether the destination accepted the chunk.

targets.expr: sum by (resource, outcome) (carddemo_batch_reject_write_seconds_sum{job="$job"}) / sum by (resource, outcome) (carddemo_batch_reject_write_seconds_count{job="$job"})

panels.title: Reject dataset chunk write elapsed time

panels.description: One observation per sign-on turn, tagged with the decision the turn reached. Split by outcome rather than aggregated because a rise in the not-found outcome and a rise in the failed-verification outcome mean different things. The tag values are the enumerated decision names, so the label cannot become high-cardinality.
panels.title: Sign-on turn elapsed time by outcome

list.description: The Prometheus scrape job label. Published by config/prometheus/prometheus.yml as job_name and stamped onto every series it collects. Hidden and single-valued because it is an interface between two files, not a user choice: that collector also scrapes itself under a second job, so every query on this dashboard is scoped by this label.
list.label: Scrape job
list.name: job

list.description: Endpoint filter for the per-endpoint row. Discovered from the data rather than hardcoded, so no endpoint path is duplicated into this file. Defaults to All, which matches every URI, so the row is populated before any selection is made.
list.label: Endpoint
list.name: uri

list.description: Batch step filter. The label name is prefixed because Spring Batch publishes its step timer through the Observation API. Defaults to All and stays empty until a job has been launched, which is expected rather than a fault.
list.label: Batch step
list.name: step
